Part 1

What interception is

The part of precipitation caught by surfaces before it reaches the ground

What is interception?

Key idea

Interception is the part of precipitation caught by the earth’s surfaces, most of which ultimately evaporates.

Which surfaces?

Vegetation, soil, litter and built surfaces.

What controls the amount?

The type, roughness and area of the surfaces, and how they interact with each other, in a forest or in an urban area.

Read the diagram

Rain either misses the canopy (direct throughfall) or lands on it. Water on the canopy fills canopy storage, then evaporates, drips off (indirect throughfall) or runs to the trunk as stemflow.

Important definitions to remember

Key idea

Water that lands on vegetation either reaches the ground (throughfall, stemflow, canopy drip) or evaporates (interception loss).

  • Interception: precipitation is caught by vegetation before it reaches the ground
  • Throughfall: water that reaches the ground directly through canopy gaps, or indirectly by dripping off leaves, stems and branches
  • Stemflow: rain intercepted by stems and branches that flows down the trunk into the soil
  • Canopy drip: some plants, especially conifers, direct water to the edge of the canopy, creating a wetter band on the ground there
  • Interception loss: evaporation from the canopy surface
  • Interception gain? Rare in the Pacific Northwest: fog condenses on pine needles, which act as condensation nuclei

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 Rain falls on a forest. Name the three ways it can reach the forest floor, and the one way it can fail to.

Reach the floor: direct throughfall, indirect throughfall / canopy drip, stemflow. Fail to: interception loss (evaporation from the canopy).

Part 2

Throughfall, leaf area and stemflow

How water passes through and down the canopy

Throughfall

  1. Throughfall
  2. Leaf area index
  3. Stemflow
Key idea

Throughfall is water falling directly or indirectly to the ground (yellow arrows). Direct throughfall is controlled by canopy coverage.

Direct throughfall

Controlled by canopy cover, measured as the leaf area index (LAI): the ratio of leaf area to ground area.

  • LAI > 1: more than one layer of leaves
  • LAI < 1: gaps allow direct throughfall

Indirect throughfall

indirect throughfall = f(LAI, canopy storage capacity, rainfall)

Canopy storage capacity: the volume of water the canopy can hold before it starts dripping. It depends on the size, area and water-holding capacity of the leaves.

Leaf area index

  1. Throughfall
  2. Leaf area index
  3. Stemflow
Key idea

LAI is the ratio of one-sided leaf area to ground area. It is unitless because it is a ratio of areas.

LAI quantifies the amount of leaf material in a canopy, and is a measure of plant growth.

Read the figures

  • LAI = 1: a 1:1 ratio of leaf area to ground area (A, right)
  • LAI > 1: leaves stack in layers (B, right: LAI = 3)
  • LAI < 1: plants cover only part of the ground (left: 0.4 and 0.8)

It changes over time

LAI differs among plant species, and changes seasonally as deciduous trees lose and regrow their leaves.

LAI varies across the planet

  1. Throughfall
  2. Leaf area index
  3. Stemflow
Key idea

LAI varies spatially by region and is highly correlated with vegetation density and abundance.

Read the maps

The highest LAI is in tropical rainforests (Amazon, Central Africa, Southeast Asia). Deserts and the poles are near zero.

The small maps show LAI month by month: northern forests green up in summer and drop in winter.

Why it matters

A higher LAI means more surface to catch and store rain, so less direct throughfall and more interception loss.

Stemflow

  1. Throughfall
  2. Leaf area index
  3. Stemflow
Key idea

Stemflow directs precipitation down branches and stems (red arrows), giving the ground around the stem extra moisture.

The amount depends on leaf shape and stem and branch architecture.

  • Like a funnel: water from a large area is delivered to a small area
  • In general, deciduous trees have more stemflow than conifers
  • As it runs down, stemflow traps air pollutants and can weather the trunk, which may change the quality of water entering the soil

Throughfall vs. stemflow

  1. Throughfall
  2. Leaf area index
  3. Stemflow
Key idea

Throughfall is usually a much bigger share of precipitation than stemflow.

Read the graph

Both increase with rainfall, but throughfall (black) climbs steeply while stemflow (pink) stays close to zero.

Why?

Stemflow is limited by the tree’s characteristics: its branches and trunk can only funnel so much. Throughfall has more room to increase with precipitation intensity.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q2 A canopy has 250 m² of leaves (one side) over 100 m² of ground. What is the LAI, and what does it tell you?

LAI = 250 / 100 = 2.5. Leaves are stacked about 2.5 layers deep, so there is little direct throughfall.

Q3 Why does LAI change through the year in a deciduous forest, and how does that change throughfall?

Trees lose leaves in autumn, so LAI drops. With fewer leaves more rain falls through as direct throughfall in winter.

Q4 Which usually delivers more water to the forest floor, throughfall or stemflow? Why?

Throughfall. Stemflow is limited by the tree’s branch and trunk architecture; throughfall keeps rising with rainfall.

Part 3

Interception gain and loss

When canopies add water, and what controls how much they take away

Interception gain (a rare event)

Key idea

Sometimes a canopy adds water: fog and cloud droplets collect on needles and drip to the ground after rain.

  • Fog drip: needles comb water from fog
  • Coniferous leaves act as condensation nuclei, promoting larger droplets that fall to the ground
  • Sharp needles are especially good at this

Think about it

Less water yield after logging? Where fog drip is important, removing trees can reduce the water reaching the ground. This is a rare event, but it happens in foggy coastal forests of the Pacific Northwest.

Interception loss

Key idea

Interception loss is the intercepted water that evaporates from vegetation surfaces and never reaches the ground.

Afforestation (planting forests) could increase ET losses by 50–100%.

Interception loss depends on two factors

  • Plant physiology
  • Meteorology

Read the study

Comparing two tree species, landscape designs using the rougher bark, lower branch angle and thinner canopy of L. tulipifera (tulip poplar) increased water losses during rainfall, which can help stormwater management.

Canopy differences

Key idea

Tree structure and type strongly influence interception loss.

Read the diagram

Interception loss (as % of rainfall) differs widely between grasses, live oak and juniper, and the litter layer under each adds its own interception.

Read the table

Hardwoods (100 years) intercept 12% of annual precipitation; white pine rises from 15% at age 10 to 26% at age 60 as the canopy grows.

(Source: Hewlett and Nutter, 1969)

Interception loss is highly climate dependent

Key idea

The percentage of rain lost to interception is highest for small storms, even though the amount lost is larger in big storms.

Meteorology and climate

  • Rainfall intensity, duration and frequency
  • Phase of precipitation (snowfall)
  • Wind speed and turbulence
  • Radiant energy balance (forest vs. grassland)
  • Regional climate

Read the graph

The solid line (amount) rises then levels off once the canopy is full. The dashed line (ratio) falls: in a light shower the canopy holds almost all the rain.

Interception has seasonal trends

Key idea

Interception changes through the seasons, and the size of the change differs among tree species.

Read the charts

Each panel is one species. Monthly interception rises and falls through the year, and the pattern is different for each species, depending on its leaves and when it carries them.

Why it matters

A water balance model that uses a single annual interception value will miss these seasonal swings.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q5 A canopy intercepts 2 mm of a 3 mm shower, and 5 mm of a 50 mm storm. Which storm had the higher interception ratio?

The shower: 2/3 ≈ 67% vs. 5/50 = 10%. Small storms lose a larger percentage to interception.

Q6 Using Table 4.1, why does interception by white pine increase as the stand ages?

Older stands have a larger, denser canopy (higher LAI and storage capacity), so they catch and evaporate more rain: 15% at 10 years to 26% at 60 years.

Part 4

Measuring and calculating interception

Gauges, collars and cranes, and three models for interception loss

Measuring interception

Key idea

Interception is found by measuring rain above the canopy and the water that reaches the ground.

  • Above-canopy: a rain gauge next to the trees, with no obstruction from nearby trees above it
  • Throughfall: rain gauges placed randomly on the forest floor
  • Stemflow: collars around a trunk that capture the water

The difference between above-canopy rain and what reaches the ground is the interception loss (next slides).

A full measurement design

Key idea

A hypothetical design to measure all possible routes of interception in a forest.

Read the diagram

  • An automatic weather station above the canopy measures gross precipitation
  • Throughfall troughs and gauges under the canopy
  • Stemflow collectors on the trunks
  • Litter and soil sensors at the bottom

Real studies rarely measure everything; they choose the routes that matter for their question.

Wind River canopy crane

Key idea

A giant crane at the Wind River Experimental Forest (Washington) gives scientists access to the top of a tall forest canopy.

From the gondola, scientists can measure many variables inside and above the canopy, including interception.

Read the diagram

The gondola hangs from a trolley on the jib and can be lowered to any height among old-growth Douglas-fir and western hemlock.

Rainfall and interception

Key idea

Interception loss is what is left of gross precipitation after throughfall and stemflow reach the ground.

Interception loss = Gross precipitation − (Throughfall + Stemflow)

Read the left graph

Daily interception (mm) rises with daily rainfall, then levels off once canopy storage is full.

Read the right diagram

Pg: gross precipitation; Ic: canopy interception; Pt: throughfall reaching the ground.

Interception loss models

Key idea

Two simple models: the general model is a water balance; empirical models fit a line to measurements.

The general model

Interception equals precipitation minus throughfall (TF) and stemflow (SF):

I = P − TF − SF

  • I: interception
  • P: precipitation above the canopy
  • TF: throughfall
  • SF: stemflow

Empirical models

Interception loss modeled as a linear function of precipitation:

I = aP + b

  • I: interception loss
  • P: gross rainfall
  • a: slope (empirical coefficient)
  • b: intercept (empirical coefficient)

Horton’s interception model (1919)

Key idea

Horton: interception loss = water evaporated during the storm + water left in canopy storage (evaporated later).

I = ∫0t E dt + S

  • I: interception loss
  • t: duration of rainfall
  • S: interception storage capacity
  • E: rate of evaporation of intercepted water

In words

Evaporation keeps removing water from wet leaves for the whole storm (the integral), and the full canopy store S evaporates after the rain stops.

Horton’s model, modified

Key idea

The modified model splits the storm at t′, the time when the canopy becomes saturated.

I = ∫0t′ E dt + ∫t′t E dt + S

  • t: duration of precipitation
  • t′: time until canopy saturation
  • S: interception storage capacity
  • E: rate of evaporation of intercepted water

Why split it?

Before saturation the canopy is still filling; after it, extra rain drips through and only evaporation keeps removing water. Treating the two periods separately is more realistic.

Challenges in estimating interception loss

Key idea

Interception loss is very hard to estimate because evapotranspiration happens at the same time and canopies are complex.

  • Vegetation complexity: bark roughness, branch inclination
  • Regression models cannot detect the non-linear relationship between interception loss and precipitation
  • Detailed hourly water balance models (the Rutter method treats the canopy as a single leaf) need lots of canopy data
  • Remote sensing struggles because the space below the canopy is hidden
  • LiDAR can build a point cloud of trees, but is expensive

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q7 Above the canopy, a gauge records 40 mm of rain. Throughfall is 28 mm and stemflow is 2 mm. What is the interception loss, as a depth and a percentage?

I = 40 − 28 − 2 = 10 mm, which is 10/40 = 25%.

Q8 An empirical model for a stand is I = 0.15P + 0.8 (mm). Estimate interception for a 20 mm storm.

I = 0.15 × 20 + 0.8 = 3.8 mm.

Q9 In Horton’s model, what does S represent, and why is it added after the integral?

S is the canopy’s interception storage capacity. It is the water still held on the leaves when rain stops, which evaporates after the storm.

Part 5

Surface storage

Water held in depressions, urban structures, and snow and ice

Depression storage

Key idea

Depression storage is water temporarily held in puddles, ditches and other depressions, which later evaporates or infiltrates.

It is the small-scale counterpart of closed drainage.

When does it fill?

As soon as rainfall intensity exceeds the local infiltration capacity, the rainfall excess begins to fill depressions.

What happens after the rain?

Water left in depressions either evaporates or infiltrates, adding to soil moisture and subsurface flow.

Read the diagram

Depression storage (circled) sits between infiltration and surface runoff: only water that overflows the depressions runs off.

Green roofs and retention ponds

Key idea

Cities build depression storage: green roofs and retention ponds hold storm water for a while.

Green roofs

The plants and soil media on a roof retain precipitation, which later evaporates or drains slowly.

Retention ponds

Built structures designed to hold water flow for a short period in response to storms, reducing peak runoff downstream.

Snow and ice

Key idea

Snow, glaciers and lake and river ice are long-term surface storage, and the timing of their melt matters.

  • Lake and river ice is freshwater storage formed by regional freezing temperatures
  • Storage is extremely important in mountain ranges, in the form of glaciers and snowpack
  • Agriculture depends on this long-term storage in the summer
  • Timing of snowmelt is critical: too early → floods, too late → drought
  • Climate change and thermal disturbances such as wildfire can shift snowmelt timing significantly

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q10 Why does depression storage only begin to fill once rainfall intensity exceeds infiltration capacity?

Until then the soil absorbs all the rain. Only the excess water ponds at the surface and collects in depressions.

Q11 Give one reason earlier snowmelt can cause problems for a Pacific Northwest farm.

Earlier melt can cause spring floods and leaves less stored water for summer irrigation, when crops need it most.
